items.prompt: What does "illegal states unrepresentable" aim for?
choices: A type that cannot hold a nonsense combination
A function that checks every input twice
A log line for every rejected call
items.explanation: The goal is that the invalid combination cannot be built at all.

items.prompt: Which option stops "sms with no phone number" earliest?
choices: A comment above the function
A type with no such shape
A log message in the sender
items.explanation: A type with no such shape stops it before the code runs.

items.prompt: A type where every field is optional usually allows:
choices: Only the combinations that were tested
Exactly one valid combination
Combinations nobody ever intended
items.explanation: Optional everywhere means many shapes, most of them unintended.

items.prompt: When the type enforces a rule, who must remember it?
choices: Nobody, the compiler holds it
Every caller, on every call
Only the on-call engineer
items.explanation: Enforcement moves from human memory to the compiler.

items.prompt: Is a comment saying "sms needs a phone number" enough?
choices: Yes, readers always follow comments
Yes, as long as the comment is in bold
No, nothing enforces a comment
items.explanation: A comment documents a rule but nothing makes callers obey it.

items.prompt: Which one is an illegal state in an alert request?
choices: Channel sms with no phone number
Channel sms with a phone number
Channel email with an email address
items.explanation: Only the sms call with no number is a combination that can never work.

items.prompt: Which catches the bad call before it ships?
choices: Waiting for a runtime error
Checking at compile time
Reading the logs next week
items.explanation: Compile time is before the code ever runs in production.

items.prompt: An interface is best described as:
choices: A list of every private field used
A style guide for naming variables
A contract between caller and code
items.explanation: A signature or request body states what callers may and may not do.

items.prompt: A signature takes a channel name plus three optional contact fields. Which statement about it is true?
choices: It rejects any call where two optional fields are both missing
It is safe as long as the channel names are written in lower case
It can express calls that no caller could ever mean to make
It prevents mismatches because each field has a descriptive name
items.explanation: Optional fields are independent of the channel, so nonsense combinations are valid values of the type. Descriptive names and casing do not constrain which combinations exist.
items.reference:
Where can the bad call be stopped?
in the type: the shape does not exist
in a deep check: only if nothing swallows it
in a comment: not enforced at all
Why: a shape that cannot be written needs no one to remember a rule.
items.learnMore:
Illegal states unrepresentable

An interface is a contract. If the contract's shape can express a call that could never be valid, then someone will eventually write it. Moving the rule into the type removes the call instead of warning about it.

Common mistake

Treating a docstring or a quiet runtime check as equivalent to a type that cannot hold the bad value.
items.reflection: Think of a form or tool you use that simply does not offer a nonsense option. What would it look like if it offered it and relied on you to avoid it?

items.prompt: A team adds a runtime check inside the sender rather than changing the type. What is still true afterwards?
choices: The bad shape can no longer be written by any caller in the code
The bad shape is rejected by the compiler on every single build
The bad shape is converted into a valid one before it is sent
The bad shape can still be written and reaches the sender
items.explanation: A runtime check detects the shape after it exists. The type still allows it, so callers can keep writing it.

items.prompt: Which redesign makes "push with no device token" unrepresentable?
choices: A push shape whose required fields include a device token
A push flag placed beside an optional device token field
A device token field that quietly defaults to an empty string
A comment above push saying the token must be set
items.explanation: Only a shape that requires the token removes the combination. An optional field, an empty default or a comment all still allow a push with no usable token.

items.prompt: Why is "callers should know better" a weak design position?
choices: Callers are unable to read documentation at all
A shape that permits mistakes will eventually receive them
Mistakes only come from callers outside the company
Documentation always contradicts the signature
items.explanation: Over enough calls and enough callers, any expressible mistake gets written. Designing the shape is cheaper than relying on every caller.

items.prompt: What does parsing produce that validating does not?
choices: A type that proves validity
A longer error message
A copy of the original raw input
items.explanation: Parsing returns a stricter type, so the check is remembered.

items.prompt: Where should the parse step live?
choices: Deep inside the last function called
At the boundary where input enters
In every function along the way
items.explanation: The edge is where loose input first appears.

items.prompt: After parsing, downstream functions should:
choices: Re-check the same rules each time
Accept the original loose input
Take the stricter type and skip re-checks
items.explanation: The type is the proof, so no further checking is needed.

items.prompt: Validating usually returns:
choices: Yes or no, with the data unchanged
A stricter type for the same data
A different function to call next
items.explanation: A validator reports a result and leaves the loose data as it was.

items.prompt: What happens when parsing fails?
choices: It passes the input on anyway
It quietly repairs the input and continues
It rejects loudly, right there
items.explanation: Failure at the boundary keeps bad data out entirely.

items.prompt: Untyped JSON from a request is best handled by:
choices: One function that builds the typed value
Reading each field directly wherever needed
Trusting the sender to always be correct
items.explanation: A single construction point keeps the rules in one place.

items.prompt: Which sentence describes parse, don't validate?
choices: Check the same loose input many times
Turn loose input into proven input once
Ignore input that looks unusual
items.explanation: The idea is to convert once and carry the proof forward.

items.prompt: Why is one parsing function easier to trust than many checks?
choices: It runs faster than any check
It never needs any tests written at all
Only one place has to be right
items.explanation: One construction point means one place to test and fix.

items.prompt: Function A returns true or false for an alert request. Function B returns a typed channel value or throws. Which statement is correct?
choices: Only A leaves later code holding something that proves validity
Only B leaves later code holding something that proves validity
Both leave later code holding a proof, since both inspect the request
Neither helps, because both run after the data has been received
items.explanation: A tells you about the data but hands back the same loose object. B returns a stricter value, so its type carries the result of the check.
items.reference:
Validate versus parse
validate: check, then keep using the loose input
parse: convert once into a type that proves validity
downstream code takes the proven type
Why: the proof travels with the data instead of being re-checked everywhere.
items.learnMore:
Parse, don't validate

Validation returns yes or no and leaves the original loose data in place, so later code cannot tell it was checked. Parsing returns a new value of a stricter type, so the check is remembered in the type.

Common mistake

Writing a validator that returns a boolean and then passing the original object on as if nothing changed.
items.reflection: Think of a ticket or badge that is checked once at the door. What would change if every room inside re-checked your identity from scratch?

items.prompt: After a boundary parse, a downstream function still re-checks that sms has a phone number. What is the best reading?
choices: The parse step ran too early and should be moved deeper
Re-checking is required whenever input originally came from JSON
The code does not trust the type, or the type is still too loose
The check is the main protection and the type is only for show
items.explanation: If the parsed type truly cannot hold the bad shape, the re-check is dead code. Needing it suggests the type did not capture the rule.

items.prompt: Which design keeps the rules for a channel in exactly one place?
choices: Every caller building the channel and checking it themselves
A shared helper that callers may call before building a channel
A document listing the rules for each channel
One parser that is the only code that builds the channel
items.explanation: If anyone can build the value directly, the rules are spread out again. Only a single construction point keeps them in one place.

items.prompt: A parser accepts an sms channel when the phone number is present but the wrong kind of value, such as a number instead of text. What does that show?
choices: The parser must check the field's type, not only its presence
The union type will catch it later without any extra work from you
Phone numbers are never worth checking at the boundary
The check should be moved to the sender to be effective
items.explanation: A parser vouches for what it returns, so it has to check the actual value. The type cannot see what the parser let through.

items.prompt: What does "fail fast" mean?
choices: Reject bad input early and loudly
Return a default and carry on
Retry the failing call until it works
items.explanation: Early, loud rejection keeps failures close to their cause.

items.prompt: What does "minimal surface area" mean?
choices: Hide every function from callers
Expose the fewest knobs that solve it
Write as little documentation as possible
items.explanation: Fewer parameters means fewer wrong combinations.

items.prompt: What does "least astonishment" ask for?
choices: A call with many hidden side effects
A call that surprises the reader
A call that does what its name says
items.explanation: Names and shapes should predict behaviour.

items.prompt: A safe default is:
choices: The behaviour you get when you say nothing
The behaviour that needs the most arguments
The behaviour nobody has tested
items.explanation: Doing nothing special should be the safe path.

items.prompt: Each extra optional parameter adds:
choices: Another test the compiler writes
Another guarantee about the result
Another way for a caller to get it wrong
items.explanation: More knobs means more combinations.

items.prompt: Where is failing fast most useful?
choices: At the edge where input arrives
Only after the response is sent
In the logging code
items.explanation: The edge is where bad input is cheapest to stop.

items.prompt: A dangerous default is one that:
choices: Needs three confirmations
Is easiest to use and risky to rely on
Is hidden in the documentation
items.explanation: If the easy path is the risky one, people take it.

items.prompt: Which move reduces the number of possible calls?
choices: Renaming a parameter to be clearer
Adding a docstring
Removing an optional parameter
items.explanation: Removing a knob removes calls that could be written.

items.prompt: A function quietly returns an empty list when the query is malformed, and callers treat that as "no results". Which move was skipped?
choices: Fail fast, so a malformed query is reported instead of looking like success
Minimal surface, since the function takes too many arguments
Least astonishment, because the name of the function is unclear
Safe defaults, since an empty list is the dangerous default
items.explanation: A malformed query and a real empty result now look identical. Rejecting the bad input at the edge keeps the two apart.
items.reference:
Four moves and what each prevents
fail fast: bad input travelling inward
minimal surface: too many knobs to get wrong
least astonishment: a call that does something unexpected
safe defaults: the dangerous path being the easy one
Why: each move removes one way a permissive interface invites a mistake.
items.learnMore:
Defensive design moves

Each move targets a specific failure. The test is not whether the move is on a list, but what breaks if you skip it for this particular interface.

Common mistake

Applying every move to every function. A tiny internal helper does not need the same care as a public API.
items.reflection: Think of a tool or appliance with a dangerous default. What would the safe default and the minimum number of buttons look like?

items.prompt: An API call has a delete option that defaults to permanent, with a trash option behind a flag. Which principle is most directly broken?
choices: Fail fast, because the call returns before deleting anything
Safe defaults, because the easy call is the destructive one
Minimal surface, because trash and permanent are both offered
Parse, don't validate, because no input was converted
items.explanation: Saying nothing gives the most dangerous behaviour. The safe option should be the one you get by default.

items.prompt: Adding a seventh optional tuning parameter to a function that already has six. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: It is harmless, because optional parameters can be left out
It improves safety, because callers can tune the behaviour
It adds more wrong calls, so it needs a real reason to exist
It has no effect, because defaults make the choice for callers
items.explanation: Each parameter multiplies the number of calls that can be written. A parameter should justify the extra misuse surface it brings.

items.prompt: A method named `save` also sends an email and clears a cache. Which principle does it break, and why does it matter?
choices: Fail fast, because the method does not throw on failure
Minimal surface, because the method has too many arguments
Safe defaults, because email should always be disabled
Least astonishment, because the name hides what it does
items.explanation: The surprise is the problem: a reader cannot know the side effects without reading the code. A name and shape should tell you what will happen.

items.prompt: What is the boolean-parameter trap?
choices: Flags whose meaning is unclear at the call site
Booleans that are too slow to compute
Booleans that cannot be set to false
items.explanation: True and false carry no names at the call site.

items.prompt: In send(id, msg, true, false), what is unclear?
choices: Which function is being called
Which flag each value belongs to
Whether the call returns a value
items.explanation: Positional booleans hide what they control.

items.prompt: What does "stringly-typed" mean?
choices: A string used in a log message
A string that is longer than usual
A bare string stands in for a set
items.explanation: The type allows any text where only a few values are valid.

items.prompt: What does the compiler say about channel: "sm" if channel is a string?
choices: Nothing, it is a valid string
It reports the typo as an error
It rewrites it to "sms" for you
items.explanation: A string type accepts any text, including typos.

items.prompt: Two booleans can be combined in:
choices: Two ways
Eight ways
Four ways
items.explanation: Each boolean has two values, so two give 2 x 2 = 4.

items.prompt: A closed set type such as email, sms or push does what?
choices: Rejects values outside the set
Accepts any text that is given
Converts unknown values silently
items.explanation: Only the listed values are allowed.

items.prompt: Which call site reads better?
choices: send(id, msg, true, false, true)
send(id, msg, Urgency.Immediate)
send(id, msg, 1, 0)
items.explanation: A named value says what it means where it is used.

items.prompt: Replacing a flag with a free-text string:
choices: Removes the ambiguity completely
Makes the compiler check the text
Moves the ambiguity without removing it
items.explanation: Free text is still unchecked and can be mistyped.

items.prompt: A function takes (userId, notify: boolean, silent: boolean). Which pair of values is the clearest sign of the boolean-parameter trap?
choices: notify true and silent false, the most common request
notify false and silent false, a call that does nothing
notify false and silent true, a request nobody makes
notify true and silent true, a combination whose meaning nobody can state
items.explanation: Two booleans allow four combinations. Notify and silent together contradict each other, so the signature admits a call with no coherent meaning.
items.reference:
What the call site shows
send(id, msg, true, false): which flag is which?
channel: "sm": typo accepted as a string
send(id, msg, Urgency.Immediate): says what it means
channel: Channel.Sms: a typo is an error
Why: naming the choice in a closed type puts the meaning and the check in the signature.
items.learnMore:
Boolean and stringly-typed traps

Two booleans give four combinations that read identically at the call site, and some are nonsense. A bare string accepts any text, so a typo compiles. Replacing both with a small closed type makes the call say what it means.

Common mistake

Replacing a boolean with a string. That moves the same ambiguity into text that the compiler does not check.
items.reflection: Think of a settings screen with several unlabeled switches. How would you redesign it so each combination is something a person could name?

items.prompt: A team changes `isUrgent: boolean` to `priority: string`. What problem remains?
choices: Any text is accepted, including typos and bad values
The call can no longer express an urgent request
The compiler now rejects the original urgent value
The function can no longer be called with one argument at all
items.explanation: A bare string has the same unchecked-input problem as before. A closed set of named values would let the compiler reject unsupported text.

items.prompt: Which change best fixes a function with `isUrgent` and `scheduledFor` that can both be set?
choices: A comment saying only one of the two should ever be set
A two-shape type: immediate, or scheduled plus a time
A third boolean that records which of the two wins
A runtime check that logs a line when both are set
items.explanation: Both fields together are a contradiction. A type with an immediate shape and a scheduled shape cannot hold both at once.

items.prompt: Where did the quiet runtime check fail in the story?
choices: It ran before any input arrived
It sat inside a broad try/catch
It was written in the wrong language
items.explanation: A catch-all handler swallowed the error it raised.

items.prompt: Moving a check to the boundary means it runs:
choices: Before inner layers see the data
After the response is sent back
Only during scheduled batch jobs
items.explanation: The boundary is the first stop for incoming data.

items.prompt: A check that is swallowed and logged quietly is:
choices: Stronger than a type
Missing in practice
Visible to every caller
items.explanation: Nobody acts on a quiet log line.

items.prompt: Which is the weakest place for a check?
choices: At the entry point of the request
In the type of the request itself
Deep inside a catch-all handler
items.explanation: Deep placement means layers of trust and possible swallowing.

items.prompt: Layers between caller and a deep check must:
choices: Re-validate or trust upstream
Copy the data into a new queue
Skip the data entirely
items.explanation: Each layer either checks again or assumes it was checked.

items.prompt: Three outcomes for the bad call are:
choices: Warning, retry, success, and a timeout
Slow, fast, cached
Type error, runtime error, silence
items.explanation: These are the three places the mistake can be caught or missed.

items.prompt: Which outcome is the worst?
choices: Silence in production
A compile error on your laptop
A failed code review comment
items.explanation: Silent failure is found only by its consequences.

items.prompt: A type error appears:
choices: At 3 a.m. during an outage
Before the code is merged
After a customer reports it
items.explanation: The compiler reports it while the code is still being written.

items.prompt: A validation check lives three calls deep, inside a handler that catches all errors and logs at debug level. What happens when the bad input reaches it?
choices: The error is caught by the handler and effectively lost
The error stops the build before the code is deployed
The error reaches the caller with a clear message
The error is converted into a valid value automatically
items.explanation: A catch-all handler treats the missing-field error like any other failure. Quiet logging means nobody sees it.
items.reference:
Three outcomes for the same bad call
type error: stopped before merge
runtime error: stopped only if someone reads the log
silence: found in production
Why: a check deep inside a catch-all handler can end up in the second or third row.
items.learnMore:
Where the check lives

A check is only as strong as its position. Placed deep, it sits behind layers that trust the data and may sit inside a handler built for another purpose. Placed at the boundary, nothing sits between the input and the rejection.

Common mistake

Assuming that adding another check inside the same function fixes a swallowed error. It runs inside the same catch-all.
items.reflection: Think of a safety check in a process you know that happens late. What would be different if it happened at the very first step?

items.prompt: Which change makes the check impossible for that handler to swallow?
choices: Raise the log level of the handler's messages to error
Add the same check a second time inside the handler
Reject at the entry, before data reaches the handler
Wrap the handler in another broad error catch
items.explanation: Only a check that runs outside the handler is out of its reach. A louder log or a duplicate check still lives inside it.

silence: found in production

items.prompt: A request passes through three layers that each assume valid input. Where is a parse step most effective?
choices: After the last layer, just before the data is sent
Inside whichever layer happens to see the error first
In a separate job that scans yesterday's requests
Before the first layer, at the point input arrives
items.explanation: A parse step helps only if it runs before anything trusts the data. Later placement lets the layers act on invalid input first.

items.prompt: A discriminated union is a type that is:
choices: One of a fixed set of shapes
Any combination of optional fields
A list of text values
items.explanation: It is one of a closed set of shapes.

items.reference:
One loose shape versus a union
loose: channel + email? + phone? + token?
union: email has an address
union: sms has a phone number

Common mistake

items.prompt: With 2 on/off fields, how many combinations?
With 4 on/off fields, how many combinations?
Each added on/off field does what to the count?
choices: Adds one
Doubles it
Leaves it unchanged
items.explanation: Each field is present or absent, so it doubles the count.

items.prompt: A union with 3 shapes has how many valid shapes?
items.explanation: One valid shape per kind.

items.prompt: Adding a field inside one shape changes the number of shapes by:
choices: Three
Zero
Seven
items.explanation: The shape count stays the same.

items.prompt: Most combinations of a permissive signature are:
choices: Carefully designed one by one
Checked by the compiler
Never intended or tested
items.explanation: Only a few of the many combinations were meant.

items.prompt: With 10 on/off fields the count is about:
choices: Just over a thousand
Roughly one hundred in total
About twenty at most
items.explanation: 2 to the power of 10 is 1,024.

items.prompt: The counting model treats each field as:
choices: A free text value of any length
A list of several named options
Either present or absent
items.explanation: It is a simplified on/off model.

items.prompt: A permissive signature has 5 independent on/off fields, and a union has 4 valid shapes. How many combinations does the permissive signature allow?
choices: 32, which is 2 to the power of 5
10, which is five fields times two
25, which is five fields squared
20, which is 5 times the 4 shapes
items.explanation: Each field doubles the count, so 5 fields give 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 32.
items.reference:
Combinations as fields are added
2 on/off fields: 4 calls
4 on/off fields: 16 calls
6 on/off fields: 64 calls
10 on/off fields: 1,024 calls
3-shape union: always 3
Why: each added on/off field doubles the count, while adding a field inside a shape adds no new shape.
items.learnMore:
Counting misuse

In the simplified model, every on/off field is present or absent, so n fields give 2 to the power of n combinations. A union's valid count equals its number of shapes, which does not change when a shape gains a field.

Common mistake

Reading the model as a prediction of real bugs. It counts possible calls, not how many are likely to be written.
items.reflection: Think of a tool with many switches. How many settings exist, and how many does anyone actually need?

items.prompt: Implement `parseSms(raw)`. If `raw.phoneNumber` is a string, return `{ kind: "sms", phoneNumber: raw.phoneNumber }`. Otherwise throw an error.
items.explanation: The function only builds the sms value when the field it needs is present, so no sms value exists without a phone number.

items.prompt: Implement `parseEmail(raw)`. If `raw.emailAddress` is a string, return `{ kind: "email", emailAddress: raw.emailAddress }`. Otherwise throw an error.
items.explanation: The email value is built only when its required field is a string, and the function throws otherwise.

items.prompt: Implement `parsePush(raw)`. If `raw.deviceToken` is a string, return `{ kind: "push", deviceToken: raw.deviceToken }`. Otherwise throw an error.
items.explanation: Checking the type, not just presence, keeps a number from being accepted as a token.

items.prompt: Implement `parseUrgency(raw)`. If `raw.kind` is `"immediate"`, return `{ kind: "immediate" }`. If it is `"scheduled"` and `raw.sendAt` is a string, return `{ kind: "scheduled", sendAt: raw.sendAt }`. Otherwise throw an error.
items.explanation: Each shape demands its own data: immediate needs none, scheduled needs a send time. Anything else is rejected.

items.prompt: Implement `parseKind(raw, allowed)`. If `raw.kind` is one of the strings in the `allowed` array, return `raw.kind`. Otherwise throw an error.
items.explanation: A closed set means anything outside it, such as a typo, is rejected at the boundary.

items.prompt: Implement `parseChannel(raw)`. `raw.kind` is `"email"`, `"sms"` or `"push"`, and each needs its own string field: `emailAddress`, `phoneNumber` or `deviceToken`. Return `{ kind, <field> }` containing only that field. Throw if `raw` is not an object, the kind is unknown, or the required field is missing or not a string.

tests.description: sms without a phone number throws

tests.expr: expect(parseChannel({ kind: "push", deviceToken: "t", phoneNumber: "+1" })).toEqual({ kind: "push", deviceToken: "t" })

items.explanation: Each kind maps to the one field it requires, that field is checked for presence and type, and a fresh object is built with only that field. The unrelated field is dropped and Maya's sms-without-phone call throws.
items.reference:
What a boundary parser must do
check the kind is one of the known ones
check the field that kind requires
build a new object with only that field
throw on anything else
Why: the parser is the only place the value is built, so every branch has to demand its own field.
items.learnMore:
Writing a boundary parser

Switch on the tag, check the single field that shape needs, and return a fresh object. Anything missing, mistyped or unknown throws. Returning a new object also drops fields that do not belong.

Common mistake

Checking that a field exists but not that it has the right type, or returning the raw input instead of a new value.
items.reflection: Think of a document you must fill in. Which fields change depending on the option you chose, and who checks that you filled in the right one?

items.prompt: A throwaway script used by two people usually needs:
choices: The full union plus a parser layer
Less ceremony than a public API
A versioned deprecation plan
items.explanation: Match the investment to the cost of being wrong.

items.prompt: Tightening a shipped public API can:
choices: Never affect anyone
Delete the old callers
Break existing callers
items.explanation: Callers written for the old shape may not compile.

items.prompt: A temporary adapter is used to:
choices: Let old callers migrate gradually
Remove the parser for new code
Hide validation errors from callers
items.explanation: It bridges old and new during the migration.

items.prompt: A closed union fits when the set of shapes is:
choices: Open to anyone
Known and fixed
Changing every day
items.explanation: A closed union lists every shape in advance.

items.prompt: A legacy sms call with no phone number, through the adapter, now:
choices: Fails immediately with a clear error
Is silently ignored
Is converted to email
items.explanation: The adapter runs the parser, so the bad call is rejected.

items.prompt: Exhaustiveness checking flags:
choices: A function that is far too long
A switch missing a union member
A variable that is never used
items.explanation: A missing case becomes a compile error.

items.prompt: Which cost does a stricter API add?
choices: Fewer checks run before merging
A larger number of valid calls
More work to define and to call
items.explanation: Callers pick a shape up front.

items.prompt: Before removing the adapter you should:
choices: Announce a removal date
Delete it quietly in a patch
Keep it forever to be safe
items.explanation: A stated removal date gives callers time.

items.prompt: A request type shipped in a public library with many users. Which rollout is safest?
choices: Replace the old shape in the next patch release without notice
Keep the loose shape and add a longer note explaining the rules
Add the safe shape beside the old one, with a deprecation date
Remove the optional fields and let callers fix their own errors
items.explanation: Existing callers need time and a working path. A silent replacement breaks them, and documentation alone does not make the loose shape safe.
items.reference:
When to pay for the safe shape
throwaway script: light touch
public API with many callers: add beside old, deprecate
open-ended set (plugins): run-time registry
growing union: exhaustiveness checking
Why: the right amount of safety depends on who calls it and what a wrong call costs.
items.learnMore:
Trade-offs in practice

A strict shape costs more to define and to call. It earns that cost where callers are many or unknown and where a wrong call is expensive. Tightening a live API is a migration, not an edit, and an adapter must still pass through the parser.

Common mistake

Replacing the old signature in place, which breaks every existing caller at once.
items.reflection: Think of a rule you could apply strictly or loosely. What would tell you which one a given situation deserves?

It cannot name a kind that does not exist at compile time
items.explanation: A union lists its shapes in advance. Open-ended kinds need run-time validation from a registry of handlers, though the principle of rejecting at the boundary stays.
